compare_blocks.title: One-minute comparison

compare_blocks.body:

Each shared preference has a boundary. Either type can run a very tight process when the duty is clear, and either can say nothing at all about a project that does not interest them.

### ENFP and ESFP: when entries fall short, which information gets trusted

In this fictional three-on-three basketball tournament, both organizers see the same nine sign-ups, the same gaps in two teams and the same court and referee schedules.

Either organizer might ask what the sign-up and attendance records confirm or look for a pattern that suggests another way to form teams. This illustrates S/N: concrete observations and experience versus patterns and possibilities. The organizers can use both when deciding whether to allow teams with students from different classes.

Either person could go to the court to verify attendance and notice something that suggests a new format. Going to the court does not distinguish the types.

The confirmed headcount helps the organizers estimate capacity. A possible team format can show where to look for more participants. Any proposed change still has to fit the same court and referee schedules.

The numbers here need their use kept straight. Sheets returned, attendance, teams withdrawn and how many referee slots can be covered are operational measures for judging whether a plan is feasible, and cannot distinguish types. What can serve as discussion material is which information the people considered at that moment, and which they set aside.

compare_blocks.body:
Boundary of use: what follows shows how two people organise the same batch of information during one tournament; it is not a way to allocate posts by type. Who suits which segment depends on past experience, actual trial and the duty at the time.

Either organizer can review the confirmed headcount and propose a different format. Agreeing who can change the rules and who will update the roster makes the next step clear.

### ENFP and ESFP: entries and teams — which end gets watched first

(Fictional scene) In the same tournament, one may make the entry point more playful: change the three columns to what you want to play and when you can come, allow one person to enter two events, and set up an on-site sign-up desk; the other may survey the ground: which periods have classes, which court is slippery, who can referee, then name people according to conditions. These two approaches are only possibly related to preference; what matters more is who owns which part and who knows these people better.

The risk of the first is an entry point opened wider than the back end can absorb; the risk of the second is that everyone recruited is a familiar face and other classes feel excluded. A workable combination sets capacity from the site conditions first, then designs the entry point to fill that capacity, each side giving a little.

A check can work like this: change the sheet into two columns — what you want to enter and when you can come — and build a cross-tab from what comes back. If one slot far exceeds court capacity, check first whether the number of courts in that slot matches the demand rather than attributing it to the entry design; if most cells are empty, check in turn the reach of the publicity, time conflicts and the appeal of the events themselves. A cross-tab suggests where to look next; it does not give the cause.

### ENFP and ESFP: a student who wants to play but fears holding others back

In a fictional tournament, a student wants to play but is worried about letting the team down. Both organizers know the same things about their experience. Either can ask what kind of participation the student wants, check which places are open and consider a short practice before the student decides.

A conversation can clarify which options appeal to the student. A practice can give everyone more information about how one option would work. Neither tells you the student’s or the organizers’ type.

If he still does not play in the end, the problem lies in the number of places and in communication, not in type. What needs discussing is who explains it and how a place is held next time, not who is better at looking after people.
compare_blocks.title: Illustrative scenarios

compare_blocks.body:
Reading S as not thinking and N as unrealistic is the most common mismatch. An ESFP will also design a completely new format, and an ENFP will also work out headcount, courts and referees in detail. Judging type by whether someone has ideas will almost certainly fail.

The second misread comes from athletic ability. Playing well and reacting fast have nothing to do with the second letter; an ENFP running hard on court and an ESFP filling in a form slowly are neither of them evidence.

The third writes it as who is better suited to being sports representative. The actual requirements split into three parts: writing the schedule and rules clearly, aligning with classes and referees, and handling last-minute changes on the day. All three are trainable, and whether someone suits it depends on which part they have done and how well, not on four letters.

The fourth treats a division of work as evidence of difference — one designs, one runs the floor reads smoothly but only turns a temporary arrangement into a type difference. Either type can do the same job, and the division follows experience, duty and how many people are present.

If the scores are close, recall whether you were referring to your own habits or to the role and duty you held in the team at the time. Retesting with the same tool in a similar situation can be compared, but the result is for reflection only, not for awarding yourself a new type.

sections.body_md:
Preference definitions follow the [Myers-Briggs official facts page](https://www.myersbriggs.com/en-us/support/mbti-facts); the type-dynamics framework follows the [Foundation's note on type dynamics](https://www.myersbriggs.org/unique-features-of-myers-briggs/type-dynamics-processes/) and the [type dynamics overview](https://www.myersbriggs.org/unique-features-of-myers-briggs/type-dynamics-overview/).

The arrangement of the four positions here, in particular the attitude of the third process, follows a common writing adopted as an editorial convention; other sources handle it differently, and this page does not present the writing as the Foundation's only reading, nor use position to predict behaviour order, areas of strength, collaboration or attraction.

The entries, the team formation and the story of that student are editorial fiction, written to illustrate how people can use the same evidence, corresponding to no real event or person.

The number of sheets returned, attendance and withdrawals are operational measures for the tournament and are not used for type judgement. Assessment results are not for ranking ability, hiring screens, allocating posts or predicting relationships, and are not a basis for evaluating anyone's performance.

The FermatMind assessment uses its own item bank and scoring, described in the [scoring and evidence note](/en/tests/mbti-personality-test-16-personality-types#method-and-evidence).
